title: The civic intelligence in building AI data centers
text:
The civic intelligence in building AI data centers
Behind the bans on and delays in data center construction lies a preference for consultation with local communities rather than an aversion to a new technology transforming society.
As a top issue in recent U.S. elections, the building of hyperscale data centers for artificial intelligence might seem to be producing a popular backlash against a technology moving at breakneck speed. The giant structures are seen by some as threatening jobs, livelihoods, and the environment. Yet a deeper consideration reveals this “techlash” is less a stance against something than a stand for something – transparency, accountability, and civilian involvement in big projects.
Voters in 10 states passed 40 out of 41 local ballot measures to constrain data center development, as the Monitor’s Story Hinckley has reported. That’s not a return to the Luddite era, nor an indication that the United States could lose its competitive edge in the global economy. Instead, it’s a sign of Americans exerting their democratic prerogative and voice.
“In a meaningful exercise of civic power, communities themselves are deciding the shape of AI’s physical footprint,” according to Sarah Hubbard of Harvard University’s Ash Center for Democratic Governance and Innovation. “Voters made clear that they want a say in decisions about technology.”
Rather than the results hindering industry growth, several analysts see them as prompting needed efforts to balance national and local priorities – and improve democratic functioning and institutional trust.
“The US needs to keep building data centers ... to process the clicks and taps that underpin modern life and to harness ... productivity gains,” columnist Thomas Black wrote recently in Bloomberg Opinion. The midterm results “give communities the upper hand in negotiating where and how they will be built.”
“The consequence ... should not be the demonization of data centers but the opportunity to build them with community concerns in mind,” Mr. Black noted.
These concerns primarily revolve around the speed and relative secrecy, or lack of clarity, under which data centers have been approved and permitted. And they are shared by voters across the political spectrum, leading to unexpected partnerships between liberals and conservatives in local communities on ballot measures.
Indications are that the industry seems willing to listen and adapt, according to political economist Matt Miller, based on his conversations with AI executives and investors. “They are working [on] ... a new framework of more generous, responsible and transparent offers to communities affected by data center construction,” Mr. Miller wrote last week.
These actions might include commitments to prevent negative impacts on water and utility supply, quality, and rates; environmental mitigation; tax contributions; training programs; and other local investments. As commentator Nicholas Kristof observed in The New York Times in September, “The backdoor means of restricting access to data centers” – through bans – “seems inefficient as well as ineffective, compared with the front-door means of improving oversight and governance.”
In today’s globally connected economy, the use of online computing power is likely to keep growing. This offers new challenges and opportunities for individuals and institutions in the world’s democracies to step up and speak up for communities and civic interests.
